claim: Rats can detect true changes in outcome values even when they occur against a background of stochastic feedback.
source: Therefore, rodents are able to learn about fundamental directional changes in value means despite stochastic fluctuations in outcome values under baseline conditions (i.e., expected uncertainty).
evidence: Demonstrated through behavioral experiments where rats (n=8) successfully changed choice behavior in response to value upshifts and downshifts while maintaining stable preferences during baseline conditions with outcome variability.

claim: All animals significantly changed their preference in response to all shifts (all p values<0.05).
source: All animals significantly changed their preference in response to all shifts (Figure 1, all p values<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data from rats showing significant preference changes during value shifts.

claim: Greater variance of outcome distribution at baseline facilitated behavioral adaptation in response to value upshifts.
source: greater variance of outcome distribution at baseline facilitated behavioral adaptation in response to value upshifts (HV vs LV difference, p=0.004)
evidence: Statistical comparison showing significant difference (p=0.004) between HV and LV conditions during upshifts.

claim: Greater variance of outcome distribution rendered animals suboptimal during downshifts.
source: but rendered animals suboptimal during downshifts (p=0.027)
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant difference (p=0.027) in performance during downshifts on HV option.

claim: The number of initiation omissions was significantly increased during downshift in value.
source: the number of omissions was significantly increased during downshifts (p=0.004)
evidence: Statistical analysis of omission data showing significant increase (p=0.004) during downshift conditions.

claim: The number of initiation omissions was significantly decreased during upshifts in value.
source: decreased during upshifts (p=0.017) in value
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant decrease (p=0.017) in omissions during upshift conditions.

claim: Task engagement was sensitive to overall environmental reward rate.
source: revealing that task engagement was sensitive to overall environmental reward rate.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of initiation omissions changing systematically with reward conditions (upshift vs downshift).

claim: Gephyrin showed uncertainty-dependent upregulation in BLA that was maximal following HV training.
source: Subsequent analyses identified uncertainty-dependent upregulation of gephyrin in BLA [between-subject ANOVA: F(2,21)=45.448, p<0.0001), that was maximal following HV training (all post hoc comparison p values<0.05).
evidence: ELISA protein expression analysis showing significant upregulation (p<0.0001) with post-hoc comparisons confirming maximal effect in HV condition.

claim: GluN1 showed robust upregulation in response to experienced reward in BLA.
source: Similarly, GluN1 showed robust upregulation in response to experienced reward in BLA [Figure 2B; F(2,21)=7.092, p=0.004; no reward vs LV p=0.045; no reward vs HV p=0.002]
evidence: ELISA analysis showing significant upregulation (p=0.004) with specific comparisons between reward and no-reward groups.

claim: GluN1 upregulation in BLA did not differ significantly between HV and LV training.
source: however post hoc analyses failed to detect a significant difference between HV and LV training (p=0.637).
evidence: Post-hoc statistical comparison showing no significant difference (p=0.637) between HV and LV conditions.

claim: In OFC, gephyrin was downregulated in response to experiences with reward in general.
source: In OFC, gephyrin was instead downregulated in response to experiences with reward in general [F(2,12)=4.445, p=0.036; no reward vs LV p=0.045; no reward vs HV p=0.042]
evidence: ELISA analysis showing significant downregulation (p=0.036) in reward conditions compared to no-reward control.

claim: Gephyrin downregulation in OFC did not depend on variability in outcome distribution.
source: and did not depend on variability in outcome distribution (post hoc comparison: HV vs LV, p=1)
evidence: Post-hoc comparison showing no significant difference (p=1) between HV and LV conditions in OFC.

claim: No changes in GluN1 were observed in OFC.
source: no changes were observed in GluN1 [F(2,21)=2.359, p=0.119].
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no significant effect (p=0.119) of reward experience on GluN1 in OFC.

claim: OFC-lesioned rats changed their option preference to a significantly lesser degree compared to control animals during upshifts on HV.
source: they changed their option preference to a significantly lesser degree compared to control animals during upshifts on HV (p=0.005)
evidence: Statistical comparison of behavioral data showing significant difference (p=0.005) between OFC-lesioned and control groups.

claim: OFC-lesioned rats changed their option preference to a significantly lesser degree compared to control animals during upshifts on LV.

source: BLA-lesioned animals changed their option preference to a lesser degree on HV upshifts (p<0.0001)

claim: BLA-lesioned animals compensated by exaggerated adaptations to HV downshifts.
source: but compensated by exaggerated adaptations to HV downshifts (p<0.0001; Figure 4A).

claim: Sham-lesioned animals demonstrated increased sensitivity to unexpected feedback compared to predictable fluctuations for both wins and losses.
source: Critically, sham-lesioned animals demonstrated increased sensitivity to unexpected outcomes compared to predictable fluctuations for both wins and losses (Figure 4B, p values <0.0001).

evidence: Win-stay/lose-shift analysis showing significant differences (p<0.001) between expected and unexpected outcomes in BLA-lesioned group.

claim: BLA-lesioned animals' sensitivity to feedback decreased overall.
source: although their sensitivity to feedback decreased overall.

claim: OFC-lesioned animals failed to distinguish expected from unexpected fluctuations.
source: In contrast, OFC-lesioned animals failed to distinguish expected from unexpected fluctuations.
evidence: Win-stay/lose-shift analysis showing no significant difference between expected and unexpected outcomes in OFC-lesioned group.

source: However, this experimental group demonstrated significantly attenuated learning during the upshift on HV (p values < 0.0001 for all sessions)
evidence: Session-by-session analysis showing highly significant differences (p<0.0001) across all five sessions during HV upshift.

claim: BLA-lesioned animals showed potentiated performance during sessions 3 through 5 on HV downshift.
source: and potentiated performance during sessions 3 through 5 on HV downshift (p values < 0.05)
evidence: Session-by-session analysis showing significant differences (p<0.05) in later sessions of HV downshift.

claim: OFC-lesioned animals demonstrated significantly slower learning during sessions 3 through 5 during upshift on HV.
source: these animals demonstrated significantly slower learning during sessions 3 through 5 during upshift on HV (p values < 0.05)
evidence: Session-by-session analysis showing significant differences (p<0.05) in later sessions of HV upshift.

source: all sessions during upshift on LV (p values < 0.05)
evidence: Session-by-session analysis showing significant differences (p<0.05) across all sessions during LV upshift.

source: and sessions 3 through 5 during downshift on LV (p values < 0.05).
evidence: Session-by-session analysis showing significant differences (p<0.05) in later sessions of LV downshift.

claim: The behavior of the control group was best captured by the dynamic learning rate model with RPE scaling proportional to expected outcome uncertainty and facilitation of learning in response to surprising feedback (Full model).
source: The behavior of the control group was best captured by the dynamic learning rate model with RPE scaling proportional to expected outcome uncertainty and facilitation of learning in response to surprising feedback (Full model; Table 1, lower BIC values indicate better fit).
evidence: Computational modeling using BIC for model comparison, with Full model showing lowest BIC value for control group.

claim: Trial-by-trial performance in BLA-lesioned animals was best fit by RW+expected uncertainty model.
source: Consistent with attenuated learning observed in animals with BLA lesions, trial-by-trial performance in these animals was best fit by RW+expected uncertainty model
evidence: Computational modeling showing RW+expected uncertainty model had lowest BIC value for BLA-lesioned group.

claim: BLA lesions caused selective loss of learning potentiation in response to surprise.
source: demonstrating selective loss of learning potentiation in response to surprise and preserved RPE scaling with expected uncertainty in these animals
evidence: Inferred from best-fit model (RW+expected uncertainty) lacking the learning rate scaling parameter present in Full model.

claim: Performance of OFC-lesioned animals was best accounted for by PH model.
source: Conversely, performance of OFC-lesioned animals was best accounted for by PH model
evidence: Computational modeling showing PH model had lowest BIC value for OFC-lesioned group.

claim: OFC-lesioned animals still increased learning rates in response to surprise but were insensitive to expected outcome uncertainty.
source: suggesting that while these animals still increased learning rates in response to surprise, they were insensitive to expected outcome uncertainty.
evidence: Inferred from best-fit model (PH) having learning rate scaling but lacking expected uncertainty parameters.

claim: Overall learning rates were reduced in OFC-lesioned animals.
source: Furthermore, the overall learning rates were reduced in OFC-lesioned animals (p=0.01 compared to the sham group).
evidence: Statistical comparison of fitted learning rate parameters showing significant difference (p=0.01).

claim: Both BLA- and OFC-lesioned animals showed significantly lower values of β (inverse temperature parameter) compared to control group.
source: Finally, we observed significantly lower values of β (inverse temperature parameter in softmax choice rule) in both BLA- and OFC-lesioned animals [F(2,21)=4.88, p=0.018; sham vs BLA: p<0.0001; sham vs OFC: p<0.0001]
evidence: Statistical comparison of fitted β parameters showing significant differences (p<0.0001) for both lesion groups.

claim: Lower β values suggest that behavior in lesioned animals is less stable, more exploratory and less dependent on the difference in learned outcome values.
source: suggesting that their behavior is less stable, more exploratory and less dependent on the difference in learned outcome values compared to control group.
evidence: Standard interpretation of inverse temperature parameter in reinforcement learning models.

claim: OFC-lesioned animals concentrated their reward port entries in the time interval corresponding to mean delays.
source: OFC-lesioned animals concentrated their reward port entries in the time interval corresponding to mean delays, suggesting that while these animals can infer the average outcomes, they fail to represent the variance (i.e., expected uncertainty).
evidence: Analysis of reward port entry distributions showing significantly lower variance in OFC-lesioned group.

claim: The distributions of reward-seeking times in BLA-lesioned rats were indistinguishable from control animals' and the true delays.
source: Whereas the distributions of reward-seeking times in BLA-lesioned rats were indistinguishable from control animals' and the true delays
evidence: Statistical comparison of reward port entry distributions showing no significant differences between BLA-lesioned and control groups.

claim: There were no significant differences in the mean of expected reward delivery times across groups.
source: There were no significant differences in the mean of expected reward delivery times across groups [F(5,42)=1.064, p=0.394].
evidence: ANOVA showing no significant effect (p=0.394) of lesion group on mean waiting times.

claim: All groups were matched in the total number of reward port entries.
source: Similarly, all groups were matched in the total number of reward port entries [F(2,21)=0.462, p=0.636; Figure 5—figure supplement 1].
evidence: ANOVA showing no significant effect (p=0.636) of lesion group on total port entries.

claim: A significant difference in variances of reward port entry distributions was detected.
source: However, a significant difference in variances of reward port entry distributions was detected [χ2(209)=4004.054, p<0.0001].
evidence: Chi-square test showing highly significant difference (p<0.0001) in variances across groups.

claim: Lesions to both the BLA and ventral OFC induced an uncertainty-avoidant phenotype.
source: In addition to their effects on value learning, lesions to both the BLA and ventral OFC induced an uncertainty-avoidant phenotype with animals in both experimental groups demonstrating reduced preference for the HV option under baseline conditions compared to the control group at the beginning of testing
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significantly reduced HV preference in both lesion groups compared to controls at baseline 1.

claim: OFC-lesioned animals increased their choices of the HV option during baseline conditions with repeated testing.
source: However, OFC-lesioned animals increased their choices of the HV option during baseline conditions with repeated testing: they were indistinguishable from controls during baselines 3 and 4 and even demonstrated a trend for higher preference than the control group during the last baseline [post hoc test, OFC vs sham: p=0.059].
evidence: Statistical comparisons showing no significant differences at baselines 3 and 4, and a trend (p=0.059) at baseline 5.

claim: Humans typically attempt to maximize benefits received per invested resource when making decisions.
source: When making decisions, humans typically attempt to maximize benefits (i.e., amount of reward) received per invested resource (i.e., money, time, physical or cognitive effort).
evidence: General statement about human decision-making behavior based on established economic theory.

claim: Animals compute economic value that takes into account rewards and costs associated with available behavioral options.
source: We, like many other animals, compute economic value that takes into account rewards and costs associated with available behavioral options and choose the alternative that is expected to result in outcomes of the highest value based on previous experiences under similar conditions (Padoa-Schioppa and Schoenbaum, 2015; Sugrue et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on value-based decision making.

claim: When outcomes of choices consistently violate expectations, new learning is needed to maximize reward procurement.
source: When the outcomes of choices consistently violate expectations, new learning is needed to maximize reward procurement.
evidence: General principle of adaptive learning based on prediction errors.

claim: Not every unexpected outcome is caused by meaningful changes in the environment.
source: However, not every unexpected outcome is caused by meaningful changes in the environment.
evidence: Conceptual statement about the nature of uncertainty and change-point detection problem.

claim: Even when conditions are stable overall, outcomes of a single experience can still be unpredictable due to small fluctuations (i.e., expected uncertainty) in reward and costs.
source: Even when conditions are stable overall, outcomes of a single experience can still be unpredictable due to small fluctuations (i.e., expected uncertainty) in reward and costs.
evidence: Definition of expected uncertainty in the context of decision making.

claim: Animals need to distinguish between true changes in the environment from stochastic feedback under otherwise stable conditions, known as the problem of change-point detection.
source: Such fluctuations complicate surprise-driven learning since animals need to distinguish between true changes in the environment from stochastic feedback under otherwise stable conditions, known as the problem of change-point detection (Courville et al., 2006; Dayan et al., 2000; Gallistel et al., 2001; Pearce and Hall, 1980; Yu and Dayan, 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to theoretical and empirical work on change-point detection.

claim: Both the basolateral amygdala (BLA) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) participate in flexible reward-directed behavior.
source: Both the basolateral amygdala (BLA) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) participate in flexible reward-directed behavior.
evidence: General statement supported by subsequent citations to specific studies.

claim: Representations of expected outcomes can be decoded from both BLA and OFC during value-based decision making.
source: Representations of expected outcomes can be decoded from both brain regions during value-based decision making (Conen and Padoa-Schioppa, 2015; Haruno et al., 2014; Padoa-Schioppa, 2007, 2009; Salzman et al., 2007; van Duuren et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Amygdala lesions render animals unable to adaptively track changes in reward availability or benefit from profitable periods in the environment.
source: Amygdala lesions render animals unable to adaptively track changes in reward availability or benefit from profitable periods in the environment (Murray and Izquierdo, 2007; Salinas et al., 1996; Salzman et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous lesion studies.

claim: BLA integrates both current reward value and long-term history information.
source: Furthermore, a recent evaluation of the accumulated literature on BLA in appetitive behavior suggests that this region integrates both current reward value and long-term history information (Wassum and Izquierdo, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Single-unit responses in BLA track surprise signals that can drive learning.
source: Importantly, single-unit responses in BLA track surprise signals (Roesch et al., 2010) that can drive learning.
evidence: Supported by citation to electrophysiological study.

claim: A functionally-intact OFC is required for adaptive responses to changes in outcome values.
source: Similarly, a functionally-intact OFC is required for adaptive responses to changes in outcome values (Elliott et al., 2000; Izquierdo and Murray, 2010; Murray and Izquierdo, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on OFC function.

claim: Impairments produced by OFC lesions have been widely attributed to diminished cognitive flexibility or inhibitory control deficits.
source: Impairments produced by OFC lesions have been widely attributed to diminished cognitive flexibility or inhibitory control deficits (Bari and Robbins, 2013; Dalley et al., 2004; Elliott and Deakin, 2005; Winstanley, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous theoretical and empirical work.

claim: The traditional view of OFC function has been challenged by observations that selective medial OFC lesions cause potentiated switching between different option alternatives.
source: However, this view has been challenged recently by observations that selective medial OFC lesions cause potentiated switching between different option alternatives, rather than a failure to disengage from previously acquired behavior (Walton et al., 2010, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing opposite effects of OFC lesions.

claim: There is increasing evidence that certain sectors of OFC may contribute outcome representations predicted by specific cues and update expectations in response to surprising feedback.
source: Indeed, there is increasing evidence that certain sectors of OFC may not exert a canonical inhibitory control over action, but may instead contribute outcome representations predicted by specific cues in the environment and update expectations in response to surprising feedback (Izquierdo et al., 2017; Marquardt et al., 2017; Riceberg and Shapiro, 2012, 2017; Rudebeck and Murray, 2014; Stalnaker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent studies on OFC function.

claim: The OFC is not required for acquisition of simple stimulus-outcome associations in Pavlovian and instrumental contexts.
source: For example, the OFC is not required for acquisition of simple stimulus-outcome associations, both in Pavlovian and instrumental context
evidence: General statement about OFC function based on accumulated literature, elaborated with specific examples.

claim: The OFC is not required for unblocking driven by differences in value when outcomes are certain and predictable.
source: or for unblocking driven by differences in value when outcomes are certain and predictable.
evidence: Statement about specific learning paradigms where OFC is not necessary.

claim: The OFC is needed for adaptive behavior that requires integration of information from different sources, particularly when current outcomes need to be compared with a history in a different context.
source: However, the OFC is needed for adaptive behavior that requires integration of information from different sources, particularly when current outcomes need to be compared with a history in a different context (or state) as in devaluation paradigms (Izquierdo et al., 2004; McDannald et al., 2011, 2005; Stalnaker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on devaluation and context-dependent learning.

claim: BLA has an important role in early learning or decision making under ambiguous outcomes in rats.
source: Similarly, as has been shown in rats, BLA has an important role in early learning or decision making under ambiguous outcomes (Hart and Izquierdo, 2017; Ostrander et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in rats.

claim: BLA seems to play a limited role in choice behavior when outcomes are known or reinforced through extended training.
source: and seems to play a limited role in choice behavior when these outcomes are known or reinforced through extended training.
evidence: Inference based on previous findings about BLA function in well-learned tasks.

claim: The functional dissociation between different OFC subregions (e.g. ventromedial vs. lateral) is presently debated.
source: Furthermore, the functional dissociation between different OFC subregions (e.g. ventromedial vs. lateral) is presently debated (Dalton et al., 2016; Elliott et al., 2000; Morris et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies examining different OFC subregions.

claim: Recently-developed computational models based on reinforcement learning and Bayesian inference principles are well suited to test for unique contributions of different brain regions to value learning under uncertainty.
source: Recently-developed computational models based on reinforcement learning (RL) (Diederen and Schultz, 2015; Khamassi et al., 2011; Preuschoff and Bossaerts, 2007) and Bayesian inference principles (Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2010) are well suited to test for unique contributions of different brain regions to value learning under uncertainty.
evidence: Supported by citations to computational modeling studies.

claim: RL models rely on learning in response to surprise, or the deviation between expected and observed outcomes (i.e., reward prediction errors, RPEs).
source: These models rely on learning in response to surprise, or the deviation between expected and observed outcomes (i.e., reward prediction errors, RPEs)
evidence: Standard description of reinforcement learning principles.

claim: The learning rate determines the degree to which prediction errors affect value estimates.
source: the learning rate, in turn, determines the degree to which prediction errors affect value estimates.
evidence: Standard description of learning rate parameter in RL models.

claim: RL principles are reflected in underlying neuronal activity.
source: Importantly, the RL principles do not only account for animal behavior, but are also reflected in underlying neuronal activity (Lee et al., 2012; Niv et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to neurophysiological studies showing RL signals in brain.

claim: Rats were presented with two choice options identical in average wait time but different in the variance of the outcome distribution.
source: To probe the effects of expected outcome uncertainty on learning in rodents, we first presented a group of naïve rats (n = 8) with two choice options identical in average wait time but different in the variance of the outcome distribution.
evidence: Description of experimental design for behavioral task.

claim: Each response option was associated with the delivery of one sugar pellet after a delay interval.
source: Each response option was associated with the delivery of one sugar pellet after a delay interval.
evidence: Description of task structure.

claim: The delays were pooled from distributions that were identical in mean, but different in variability (low vs high: LV vs HV; ~N(µ, σ): μ = 10 s, σHV=4s σLV=1 s).
source: The delays were pooled from distributions that were identical in mean, but different in variability (low vs high: LV vs HV; ~N(µ, σ): μ = 10 s, σHV=4s σLV=1 s).
evidence: Specification of delay distributions used in the task.

claim: Rats experienced value upshifts (delay mean was reduced to 5 s with variance kept constant) and downshifts (delay mean was increased to 20 s) on each option independently.
source: Following the establishment of stable performance (defined as no statistical difference in any of the behavioral parameters across three consecutive testing sessions, including choice and initiation omissions, average response latencies and option preference), rats experienced value upshifts (delay mean was reduced to 5 s with variance kept constant) and downshifts (delay mean was increased to 20 s) on each option independently, followed by return to baseline conditions (Figure 1A,B; Video 1, Video 2).
evidence: Description of experimental manipulations in the task.

claim: Each shift and baseline phase lasted five 60-trial testing sessions.
source: Each shift and baseline phase lasted five 60-trial testing sessions
evidence: Description of experimental timeline.

claim: The total duration of the main task was 43 testing days for each animal.
source: therefore, the total duration of the main task was 43 testing days for each animal.

claim: Post-hoc analyses revealed no differences in preference at baseline conditions across assessments.
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed no differences in preference at baseline conditions across assessments [F(3.08, 21.57)=0.98, p=0.422; Greenhouse-Geisser corrected]
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no significant differences (p=0.422) across baseline phases.

claim: Rats were able to infer mean option values (wait times) and maintain stable choice preferences despite variability in outcomes.
source: suggesting that rats were able to infer mean option values (wait times) and maintain stable choice preferences despite variability in outcomes.
evidence: Inference from stable baseline preferences despite outcome variability.

claim: The effects of asymmetric responses to shifts may be explained by a hyperbolic nature of delay-discounting across species.
source: These effects may be explained by a hyperbolic nature of delay-discounting across species (Freeman et al., 2009; Green et al., 2013; Hwang et al., 2009; Mazur and Biondi, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2015; Rachlin et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on delay discounting and theoretical explanation.

claim: Experience with different levels of outcome uncertainty would induce long-term neuroadaptations, affecting the response to the same magnitude of surprise signals.
source: We hypothesized that experience with different levels of outcome uncertainty would induce long-term neuroadaptations, affecting the response to the same magnitude of surprise signals.
evidence: Stated hypothesis motivating protein expression experiments.

claim: Gephyrin is a reliable proxy for membrane-inserted GABAA receptors mediating fast inhibitory transmission.
source: Specifically, we assessed expression of gephyrin (a reliable proxy for membrane-inserted GABAA receptors mediating fast inhibitory transmission; [Chhatwal et al., 2005; Tyagarajan et al., 2011])
evidence: Supported by citations to studies validating gephyrin as a marker for GABAA receptors.

claim: GluN1 is an obligatory subunit of glutamate NMDA receptors.
source: and GluN1 (an obligatory subunit of glutamate NMDA receptors; [Soares et al., 2013])
evidence: Supported by citation to study on NMDA receptor structure.

claim: Three separate groups of animals were trained to respond to visual stimuli on a touchscreen to procure a reward after variable delays, with one group under LV conditions, one under HV, and one control group receiving no rewards.
source: Three separate groups of animals were trained to respond to visual stimuli on a touchscreen to procure a reward after variable delays. The values of outcomes were identical to our task described above but no choice was given. One group was trained under LV conditions, the second under HV (matched in total number of rewards received), and the third control group received no rewards (n = 8 in each group, total n = 24).
evidence: Description of experimental design for protein expression study.

claim: The focus on NMDA instead of AMPA receptors was based on previous evidence demonstrating dissociable effects of ionotropic glutamate receptors in delay-based decision making.
source: Given the limited amount of tissue, we focused on NMDA instead of AMPA receptors based on previous evidence demonstrating dissociable effects of ionotropic glutamate receptors in delay-based decision making (Yates et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study and practical constraint of tissue availability.

claim: Both the BLA and OFC undergo unique patterns of neuroadaptations in response to experience with variability.
source: Therefore, both the BLA and OFC undergo unique patterns of neuroadaptations in response to experience with variability, suggesting that these brain regions may play complementary, yet dissociable, roles in value learning under outcome uncertainty.
evidence: Summary inference from protein expression data showing different patterns in BLA vs OFC.

claim: Rodents exhibit behavioral complexity on the uncertainty task that allows assessment of causal contributions of BLA and OFC.
source: Given the behavioral complexity that rodents exhibit on our task, we were able to directly test the causal contributions of the BLA and ventromedial OFC to value learning under conditions of expected uncertainty in outcome distribution.
evidence: Statement justifying lesion experiments based on behavioral results.

claim: Lesion sites for BLA and OFC are shown in Figure 3.
source: The results of lesion studies (lesion sites are shown in Figure 3) were in line with predictions suggested by protein data.

claim: Lesion results were in line with predictions suggested by protein data.
source: The results of lesion studies (lesion sites are shown in Figure 3) were in line with predictions suggested by protein data.

claim: Maximal changes in option preference in response to shifts were analyzed to control for potential effects of brain lesions on choice behavior under baseline conditions.
source: Because we were primarily interested in the contributions of the BLA and OFC to surprise-driven learning, we first analyzed the maximal changes in option preference in response to up- and downshifts. This analysis allowed us to control for potential effects of brain lesions on choice behavior under baseline conditions in our task.

claim: BLA-lesioned animals were indistinguishable from controls during the shifts on LV option.
source: BLA-lesioned animals were indistinguishable from controls during the shifts on LV option.
evidence: Statistical comparisons showing no significant differences between BLA-lesioned and control groups during LV shifts.

claim: No deficits in basic reward learning were observed in either the BLA- or OFC-lesioned animals.
source: Despite these differences in responses to shifts in value under conditions of uncertainty, we did not observe any deficits in basic reward learning in either the BLA- or OFC-lesioned animals, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

source: Our surgeries took place prior to any exposure to the testing apparatus or behavioral training.

claim: Both lesioned groups were indistinguishable from controls at early stages of the task.
source: Both lesioned groups were indistinguishable from controls at early stages of the task.

claim: Animals in all groups took similar number of days to learn to nosepoke visual stimuli on the touchscreen to receive sugar rewards.
source: Animals in all groups took similar number of days to learn to nosepoke visual stimuli on the touchscreen to receive sugar rewards (p=0.796)
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference (p=0.796) across groups.

claim: Animals in all groups took similar number of days to learn to initiate a trial.
source: and to initiate a trial (p=0.821).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference (p=0.821) across groups.

claim: There were no group differences in responses to the introduction of a 5 s delay interval during pre-training.
source: There were no group differences in responses to the introduction of a 5 s delay interval during pre-training (p=0.518)
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference (p=0.518) across groups.

claim: Rats in the experiment increased learning rates in response to surprise to maximize reward acquisition rate, but only if unexpected outcomes were not likely to result from value fluctuations under otherwise stable conditions.
source: Therefore, rats in our experiment increased learning rates in response to surprise to maximize reward acquisition rate, but only if unexpected outcomes were not likely to result from value fluctuations under otherwise stable conditions.
evidence: Inference from best-fit computational model (Full model) for control group.

claim: BLA lesions preserved RPE scaling with expected uncertainty.
source: demonstrating selective loss of learning potentiation in response to surprise and preserved RPE scaling with expected uncertainty in these animals, leading to slower learning compared to intact animals during the shifts on HV option.

claim: Inability to ignore meaningless fluctuations in outcomes would lead to unstable choice behavior and attenuated learning in OFC-lesioned animals.
source: Due to the lack of prediction error scaling based on the variability in experienced outcomes, OFC-lesioned animals treated every surprising event as indicative of a fundamental change in the value distribution and updated their expectations, rendering trial-by-trial value representations noisier, preventing consistent changes in preference. Because the delay distributions encountered during baseline and shift conditions in our task partially overlapped, inability to ignore meaningless fluctuations in outcomes would lead to unstable choice behavior and attenuated learning.
evidence: Theoretical explanation connecting model results to behavioral impairments.

claim: Increased reliance on win-stay/lose-shift strategy is highly suboptimal under stochastic environmental reward conditions.
source: Note that increased reliance on this strategy is highly suboptimal under stochastic environmental reward conditions (Faraut et al., 2016; Imhof et al., 2007; Worthy et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on decision strategies.

claim: The results are in agreement with previous findings demonstrating increased switching and inconsistent economic preferences following ventral OFC lesions in monkeys.
source: These results are in agreement with previous findings demonstrating increased switching and inconsistent economic preferences following ventral OFC lesions in monkeys (Walton et al., 2010, 2011).
evidence: Comparison with cited previous studies showing similar effects.

claim: Lesions to ventromedial prefrontal cortex in humans render subjects unable to make consistent preference judgments.
source: Similarly, lesions to ventromedial prefrontal cortex, encompassing the ventral OFC, in humans render subjects unable to make consistent preference judgments (Fellows and Farah, 2003, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to human lesion studies.

claim: Human subjects with OFC damage cannot distinguish between degrees of uncertainty.
source: Importantly, human subjects with OFC damage cannot distinguish between degrees of uncertainty (Hsu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to human lesion study.

claim: Previous work has implicated OFC in prediction of reward timing.
source: Similarly, previous work has implicated this brain region in prediction of reward timing (Bakhurin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: OFC-lesioned animals can infer the average outcomes but fail to represent the variance (i.e., expected uncertainty).
source: suggesting that while these animals can infer the average outcomes, they fail to represent the variance (i.e., expected uncertainty).
evidence: Inference from reward port entry distribution analysis showing concentrated entries around mean delay.

claim: These findings are consistent with emerging evidence that more ventromedial regions, unlike lateral, OFC may be critical for decision making involving outcome uncertainty, but not response inhibition or impulsive choice behavior.
source: These findings are consistent with emerging evidence that more ventromedial regions, unlike lateral, OFC may be critical for decision making involving outcome uncertainty, but not response inhibition or impulsive choice behavior as suggested previously (Stopper et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison with cited study on OFC subregion dissociations.

claim: Medial OFC lesions or inactivations induce analogous effects in probabilistic reversal learning tasks where surprising changes occur against background of stochastic outcomes.
source: Although frequently framed as a deficit in inhibitory control (Bari and Robbins, 2013; Dalley et al., 2004; Elliott and Deakin, 2005), medial OFC lesions or inactivations induce analogous effects in probabilistic reversal learning tasks where surprising changes in the reward distribution occur against the background of stochastic outcomes during the baseline conditions.
evidence: Comparison with previous studies on reversal learning, with citations.

claim: A recent study in rodents systematically compared the contributions of five different regions of the frontal cortex to reversal learning and revealed unique contributions of the OFC to successful performance under probabilistic, but not deterministic conditions.
source: For example, a recent study in rodents systematically compared the contributions of five different regions of the frontal cortex to reversal learning (Dalton et al., 2016). The results revealed unique contributions of the OFC to successful performance under probabilistic, but not deterministic conditions.
evidence: Supported by citation to comparative study of frontal cortex regions.

claim: Inactivations of the medial OFC impaired both the acquisition and reversal phases in probabilistic tasks.
source: Intriguingly, inactivations of the medial OFC impaired both the acquisition and reversal phases, suggesting that this subregion might be critical for many types of reward learning under conditions of expected outcome uncertainty.
evidence: Supported by reference to findings from Dalton et al., 2016 study.

claim: Lesions in the present study also intruded on medial OFC.
source: Since our lesions also intruded on medial OFC, our present observations are in agreement with these findings
evidence: Statement about lesion extent based on histological analysis.

claim: One of the normal functions of more ventromedial sectors of OFC might be to stabilize value representations by adjusting responses to surprising outcomes based on expected outcome uncertainty.
source: and suggest that one of the normal functions of more ventromedial sectors of OFC might be to stabilize value representations by adjusting responses to surprising outcomes based on expected outcome uncertainty.
evidence: Theoretical interpretation synthesizing current findings with previous literature.

claim: Intact performance in OFC-lesioned animals during training to respond for rewards is similar to previous work showing OFC is not required for acquisition of simple stimulus-outcome associations.
source: Similar to previous work demonstrating that the OFC is not required for acquisition of simple stimulus-outcome associations or for unblocking driven by differences in value when outcomes are certain and predictable (Izquierdo et al., 2004; McDannald et al., 2011, 2005; Stalnaker et al., 2015), we observed intact performance in OFC-lesioned animals during training to respond for rewards.
evidence: Comparison with cited previous studies showing similar pattern of results.

claim: It has been previously proposed that the OFC may provide value expectations that can be used to calculate RPEs to drive learning under more complex task conditions.
source: It has been previously proposed that the OFC may provide value expectations that can be used to calculate RPEs to drive learning under more complex task conditions (Schoenbaum et al., 2011a, Schoenbaum et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical proposals about OFC function.

claim: The observations are generally consistent with the view that OFC provides value expectations, and add a nuanced perspective that representations include information about expected uncertainty.
source: Although this initial proposal was based on findings after targeting more lateral OFC subregions, our observations are generally consistent with this view and add a nuanced perspective. Specifically, if the OFC is needed to provide expectations about the value to which the observed outcomes are then compared, lesions of this brain region may result in attenuated learning driven by violation of expectations. The results of computational modeling in our work revealed a reduction in learning rates in OFC-lesioned animals consistent with this account. Yet our data provide further evidence that the representations of expected outcomes in ventral OFC are not limited to a single-point estimate of value, but also include information about expected uncertainty of variability in outcomes.
evidence: Synthesis of current findings with previous theoretical framework, adding new perspective.

claim: OFC representations of expected outcomes include information about expected uncertainty that allows animals to assess whether surprising events are meaningful and informative.
source: This would allow an animal not only to detect if the outcomes violate expectations, but also to assess whether such surprising events are meaningful and informative to the current state of the world. If such events are important, an animal will shift its behavior, but if they may have occurred by chance, choices should remain unchanged.
evidence: Theoretical explanation of functional role of uncertainty representations in OFC.

claim: It has been suggested that the OFC represents an animal's current location within an abstract cognitive map of the task.
source: Finally, more recently it has also been suggested that the OFC represents an animal's current location within an abstract cognitive map of the task it is facing (Chan et al., 2016; Schuck et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2014), particularly when task states are not signaled by external sensory information, but rather need to be inferred from experience.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent theoretical and empirical work on OFC cognitive maps.

claim: Animals may represent different conditions (stable environment vs. shifted value) as separate states in the task.
source: In our task, animals may similarly represent different conditions, stable environment vs. shifted value, as separate states.
evidence: Speculation about how cognitive map framework applies to current task.

claim: Attenuated learning may result from state misrepresentations in OFC-lesioned animals.
source: Attenuated learning may result from state misrepresentations, where an animal incorrectly infers that it is currently in a stable environment and persists with the previous choice policy, despite the shift in value.
evidence: Theoretical explanation connecting state representation framework to observed behavioral deficits.

claim: Neuronal activity in the lateral OFC organizes the task space according to the sequence of behaviorally significant events, or trial epochs.
source: As has been reported recently, neuronal activity in the lateral OFC organizes the task space according to the sequence of behaviorally significant events, or trial epochs.
evidence: Reference to recent findings (Lopatina et al., 2017) on lateral OFC function.

claim: Neural ensembles in more medial OFC do not track the sequence of events, but instead segregate between states depending on the trial value.
source: Conversely, neural ensembles in more medial OFC do not track the sequence of the events, but instead segregate between states depending on the trial value (Lopatina et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to study showing functional dissociation within OFC.

claim: Ventromedial OFC may be especially well-positioned to encode upshifts and downshifts in value on long timescales.
source: In our study, ventromedial OFC may be especially well-positioned to encode upshifts and downshifts in value on long timescales, and loss of this function could cause an inability to recover appropriate state representations at the time of option choice.
evidence: Speculation about specific role of ventromedial OFC based on current findings and previous literature.

claim: Current results implicate the OFC in representing fine-grained value distributions, including the expected uncertainty in outcomes.
source: Taken together with previous findings, our results implicate the OFC in representing fine-grained value distributions, including the expected uncertainty in outcomes (that may be task state-dependent).
evidence: Summary synthesis of current findings with previous literature.

claim: Animals with OFC lesions over-rely on the average cached value, lacking access to the complex outcome distribution.
source: Consequently, lacking access to the complex outcome distribution, animals with OFC lesions over-rely on the average cached value.
evidence: Inference from reward port entry data showing concentration around mean delays.

claim: Suboptimal performance during even two or three sessions means BLA-lesioned animals are less efficient at reward procurement for 120-180 experiences.
source: Note that suboptimal performance during even two or three sessions in our task (each session lasting 60 trials) means that BLA-lesioned animals are less efficient at reward procurement for 120–180 experiences.
evidence: Calculation based on session structure to emphasize practical significance.

claim: In naturalistic settings, early-learning impairment can have detrimental consequences.
source: In naturalistic settings, such an early-learning impairment can have detrimental consequences.
evidence: Speculation about ecological significance of observed deficits.

claim: BLA-lesioned animals were less likely to adopt the win-stay/lose-shift strategy compared to the control group, demonstrating decreased sensitivity to surprising outcomes.
source: In agreement with the results of computational modeling, BLA-lesioned animals were less likely to adopt the win-stay/lose-shift strategy compared to the control group, demonstrating decreased sensitivity to surprising outcomes.
evidence: Win-stay/lose-shift analysis showing lower scores in BLA-lesioned group.

claim: The lack of learning facilitation can account for reduced changes in preference in response to HV upshifts in BLA-lesioned animals.
source: Whereas the lack of learning facilitation can account for reduced changes in preference in response to HV upshifts in BLA-lesioned animals, it may seem at odds with potentiated responses to downshifts on this option.
evidence: Theoretical explanation connecting model results to behavioral pattern.

claim: Control animals potentiate their learning in response to highly surprising outcomes, leading to greater behavioral adaptations in the first few sessions during the shifts.
source: Our computational modeling results suggest that control animals potentiate their learning in response to highly surprising outcomes, which leads to greater behavioral adaptations in the first few sessions during the shifts.
evidence: Inference from best-fit model (Full model) for control group showing learning rate scaling.

claim: In BLA-lesioned animals, learning facilitation function is lost, and learning proceeds at the same rate.
source: In BLA-lesioned animals, this function is lost, and learning proceeds at the same rate.
evidence: Inference from best-fit model (RW+expected uncertainty) lacking learning rate scaling parameter.

claim: Hyperbolic discounting leads to a larger impact of short delays on behavior.
source: Firstly, as discussed earlier hyperbolic discounting leads to a larger impact of short delays on behavior.
evidence: Application of established principle of delay discounting to explain behavioral pattern.

claim: Immediate or short-delayed rewards encountered during upshift on HV option will potentiate learning in control animals early on during the shift, but fail to do so in BLA lesioned animals.
source: Immediate or short-delayed rewards encountered during upshift on HV option will potentiate learning in control animals early on during the shift, but fail to do so in BLA lesioned animals.
evidence: Theoretical explanation combining hyperbolic discounting with learning facilitation deficit.

claim: During the downshift on HV option, as delays get longer, differences in waiting times become less meaningful as there is a smaller effect of larger delays on perceived outcome values.
source: During the downshift on HV option, as delays get longer, differences in waiting times become less meaningful as there is a smaller effect of larger delays on perceived outcome values.
evidence: Application of hyperbolic discounting principle to explain asymmetric effects.

claim: Learning will be potentiated, but only briefly in control animals during HV downshift, but will still proceed linearly in BLA-lesioned rats.
source: Thus, learning will be potentiated, but only briefly in control animals, but will still proceed linearly in BLA-lesioned rats.
evidence: Theoretical explanation for observed behavioral pattern during downshifts.

claim: Potentiated responses to downshifts on HV option in BLA-lesioned group may result from uncertainty avoidance interacting with surprise-driven learning.
source: Additionally, potentiated responses to downshifts on HV option in this group may result from uncertainty avoidance interacting with surprise-driven learning.
evidence: Speculation about interaction between two observed effects in BLA-lesioned animals.

claim: A consistent increase in uncertainty aversion was observed in BLA-lesioned animals.
source: Indeed, we observed a consistent increase in uncertainty aversion in BLA-lesioned animals.
evidence: Reference to baseline preference data showing reduced HV preference in BLA-lesioned group.

claim: Computational models did not include an explicit uncertainty avoidance parameter as the primary interest was in exploring alterations in learning.
source: Our computational models did not include an explicit uncertainty avoidance parameter as we were primarily interested in exploring alterations in learning.
evidence: Statement about modeling choices and limitations.

claim: Previous findings have implicated the BLA in updating reward expectancies when predictions and outcomes are incongruent and facilitating learning in response to surprising events.
source: Previous findings have implicated the BLA in updating reward expectancies when the predictions and outcomes are incongruent and facilitating learning in response to surprising events (Ramirez and Savage, 2007; Savage et al., 2007; Wassum and Izquierdo, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on BLA function.

claim: Predictive value learning in the amygdala involves a neuronal signature that accords with an RL algorithm.
source: Indeed, predictive value learning in the amygdala involves a neuronal signature that accords with an RL algorithm (Dolan, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to review on amygdala and reinforcement learning.

claim: Single-unit responses in the BLA correspond to the unsigned prediction error signals.
source: Specifically, single-unit responses in the BLA correspond to the unsigned prediction error signals (Roesch et al., 2010) that are necessary for learning rate scaling in both RL and Bayesian updating models.
evidence: Supported by citation to electrophysiological study and connection to computational models.

claim: The BLA utilizes positive and negative prediction errors to boost cue processing, potentially directing attention to relevant stimuli and potentiating learning.
source: The BLA utilizes positive and negative prediction errors to boost cue processing, potentially directing attention to relevant stimuli and potentiating learning (Chang et al., 2012; Esber and Holland, 2014) as demonstrated in downshift procedures with reductions in reward amount.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on BLA function in learning.

claim: BLA effects are frequently interpreted as surprise-induced enhancement of cue associability.
source: These effects are frequently interpreted as surprise-induced enhancement of cue associability.
evidence: Statement about common theoretical interpretation in the literature.

claim: A similar computational role for the amygdala has been proposed based on Pavlovian fear conditioning in humans, where cue-shock associations were also probabilistic.
source: Notably, a similar computational role for the amygdala has been proposed based on Pavlovian fear conditioning in humans, where cue-shock associations were also probabilistic, highlighting the general role for the amygdala in fine-tuning learning according to the degree of surprise (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to human fear conditioning study.

claim: The contribution of the BLA is apparent for both appetitive and aversive outcomes, for cues in different sensory modalities, and is not limited to changes in outcome contingencies, but also supports learning about surprising changes in delay costs.
source: Taken together, the accumulated literature suggests that this contribution of the BLA is apparent for both appetitive and aversive outcomes, for cues in different sensory modalities, and as we demonstrate here, the role is not limited to changes in outcome contingencies, but also supports learning about surprising changes in delay costs.
evidence: Synthesis of current findings with previous literature to generalize BLA function.

claim: Previous findings demonstrated that lesions or inactivations of the BLA shift the behavior away from uncertain options and promote choices of safer outcomes.
source: Similarly, previous findings demonstrated that lesions or inactivations of the BLA shift the behavior away from uncertain options and promote choices of safer outcomes (Ghods-Sharifi et al., 2009; Zeeb and Winstanley, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on BLA and risk preference.

claim: Inactivations of the medial OFC have been shown to produce consistent shifts toward the uncertain option.
source: However, inactivations of the medial OFC have been shown to produce consistent shifts toward the uncertain option (Winstanley and Floresco, 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on OFC and risk preference.

claim: OFC-lesioned animals progressively increased their preference for HV option with experience, suggesting that the effects on stable choice preference depend critically on the timing of OFC manipulations.
source: Despite demonstrating pronounced risk-aversion at the beginning of the task, OFC-lesioned animals in our experiments progressively increased their preference for HV option with experience, suggesting that the effects on stable choice preference depend critically on the timing of OFC manipulations.
evidence: Inference from longitudinal baseline preference data showing change over time in OFC-lesioned group.

claim: Both BLA and ventral OFC are causally involved in decision making and value learning under conditions of outcome uncertainty.
source: In summary, we show that both BLA and ventral OFC are causally involved in decision making and value learning under conditions of outcome uncertainty.
evidence: Summary statement synthesizing all lesion experiment results.

claim: Functionally-intact BLA is required for facilitation of learning in response to surprise.
source: Functionally-intact BLA is required for facilitation of learning in response to surprise
evidence: Summary of BLA lesion effects based on computational modeling and behavioral data.

claim: Ventral OFC is necessary for an accurate representation of outcome distributions to stabilize value expectations and maintain choice preferences.
source: whereas ventral OFC is necessary for an accurate representation of outcome distributions to stabilize value expectations and maintain choice preferences.
evidence: Summary of OFC lesion effects based on computational modeling, reward port entry data, and behavioral data.

claim: Volatile reward statistics were one of the central characteristics of ancestral habitats, favoring the selection of behavioral phenotypes that are able to cope with uncertainty.
source: Volatile reward statistics were one of the central characteristics of ancestral habitats, favoring the selection of behavioral phenotypes that are able to cope with uncertainty (Emery, 2006; Potts, 2004; Steppan et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to evolutionary biology literature.

claim: Most mammals are able to learn higher-order statistics of the environment.
source: Most mammals are able to learn higher-order statistics of the environment (Cikara and Gershman, 2016; Gershman and Niv, 2010; Niv et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on statistical learning.

claim: Mammals optimize learning rates based on the degree of uncertainty.
source: and optimize learning rates based on the degree of uncertainty (Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2010; Payzan-LeNestour and Bossaerts, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on adaptive learning rates.

claim: Most studies have been carried out in the context of probabilistic feedback, where stochasticity in outcomes is driven by reward omission in a subset of trials.
source: Until recently, most of the studies have been carried out in the context of probabilistic feedback, where stochasticity in outcomes is driven by reward omission in a subset of trials.
evidence: Statement about the state of the literature prior to current work.

claim: Unlike in laboratory tasks, uncertainty in naturalistic settings is not limited to probabilistic binary outcomes, but also includes variability in delays and effortful costs required to obtain the desired rewards.
source: Unlike in laboratory tasks, uncertainty in naturalistic settings is not limited to probabilistic binary outcomes, but also includes variability in delays and effortful costs required to obtain the desired rewards.
evidence: Conceptual statement about ecological validity and motivation for current task design.

claim: The present work provides the first evidence that rats can detect and learn about the true changes in outcome values even when they occur against a background of stochastic delay costs.
source: In the present work, we developed a delay-based task for rats to investigate the effects of expected outcome uncertainty on value learning. Our results provide the first evidence that rats can detect and learn about the true changes in outcome values even when they occur against a background of stochastic delay costs.
evidence: Summary of main behavioral finding from initial experiment.

claim: Animals successfully changed their choice behavior in response to directional shifts in delay distributions to maximize the rate of reward acquisition.
source: In our task, animals successfully changed their choice behavior in response to directional shifts in delay distributions (i.e., value up- and downshifts) to maximize the rate of reward acquisition, while maintaining stable choice preferences despite variability in outcomes under baseline conditions.
evidence: Summary of behavioral results showing adaptive learning.

claim: The delays in the task were normally distributed, but the perceived value distributions may be skewed due to hyperbolic discounting.
source: Specifically, the delays in our task were normally distributed, but the perceived value distributions may be skewed.
evidence: Theoretical explanation for asymmetric learning effects based on delay discounting.

claim: The HV option produces a greater proportion of immediate or short-delayed rewards, and therefore more valuable outcomes.
source: Since the HV option produces a greater proportion of immediate or short-delayed rewards, and therefore more valuable outcomes, it may generally be easier for animals to detect upshifts on this option.
evidence: Inference from delay distribution properties and hyperbolic discounting.

claim: More immediate rewards may be more salient and/or more preferred.
source: These more immediate rewards may be more salient and/or more preferred.
evidence: Speculation about psychological mechanisms underlying observed effects.

claim: During downshifts as delays get longer, differences in waiting time become less meaningful and the LV option that produces more delays of similar value could promote faster learning about worsening of reward conditions.
source: Conversely, during the downshifts as delays get longer, differences in waiting time become less meaningful and the LV option that produces more delays of similar value could promote faster learning about worsening of reward conditions.
evidence: Theoretical explanation for asymmetric effects based on hyperbolic discounting.

claim: One of the most difficult challenges faced by an animal learning in an unstable habitat is correctly distinguishing between true changes in the environment that require new learning from stochastic feedback under mostly stable conditions.
source: One of the most difficult challenges faced by an animal learning in an unstable habitat is correctly distinguishing between true changes in the environment that require new learning from stochastic feedback under mostly stable conditions.
evidence: Conceptual statement about the change-point detection problem.

claim: The problem of change-point detection has long been studied in relation to modulation of learning rates in RL and Bayesian learning theory.
source: Indeed, the problem of change-point detection has long been studied in relation to modulation of learning rates in RL and Bayesian learning theory (Behrens et al., 2007; Courville et al., 2006; Dayan et al., 2000; Gallistel et al., 2001; Pearce and Hall, 1980; Pearson and Platt, 2013; Yu and Dayan, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and computational work.

claim: Long-term neuroadaptations in response to experience with outcome uncertainty may benefit learning by altering signal-to-noise processing.
source: Long-term neuroadaptations in response to experience with outcome uncertainty may benefit learning by altering signal-to-noise processing (Hoshino, 2014; Liguz-Lecznar et al., 2015; Rössert et al., 2011), such that only those surprising events that exceed the levels of expected variability in the environment produce neuronal responses and affect behavior.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on neural plasticity and signal processing, with theoretical explanation.

claim: Adaptations to expected uncertainty at the protein level are likely to diminish responses to subsequent trial-by-trial surprise signals in BLA.
source: Adaptations to expected uncertainty at the protein level are likely to diminish responses to subsequent trial-by-trial surprise signals in BLA.
evidence: Inference from protein expression data showing uncertainty-dependent upregulation.

claim: Concurrent increases in the sensitivity to excitation and inhibition benefit signal-to-noise processing.
source: Concurrent increases in the sensitivity to excitation and inhibition benefit signal-to-noise processing, providing further evidence in support of this view (Hoshino, 2014; Liguz-Lecznar et al., 2015; Rössert et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on neural signal processing.

claim: To detect environmental changes, animals need to compare current prediction errors to the levels of expected outcome uncertainty.
source: To detect environmental changes, animals need to compare current prediction errors to the levels of expected outcome uncertainty.
evidence: Theoretical statement about computational requirements for change detection.

claim: Previous work has shown that GABA-ergic interneurons in BLA gate the information flow and determine the signal intensity that is passed to postsynaptic structures.
source: Previous work has shown that GABA-ergic interneurons in BLA gate the information flow and determine the signal intensity that is passed to postsynaptic structures (Wolff et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on BLA circuit function.

claim: The intrinsic excitability of pyramidal neurons and activity of interneurons in the BLA are shaped by reward experiences, possibly via a dopamine-dependent mechanism.
source: The intrinsic excitability of pyramidal neurons (Motanis et al., 2014; Paton et al., 2006) and activity of interneurons in the BLA are shaped by reward experiences, possibly via a dopamine-dependent mechanism (Chu et al., 2012; Merlo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on BLA plasticity and neuromodulation.

claim: Upregulation of functional GABAA receptors may decrease sensitivity to surprising events when outcome variability is high even under mostly stable conditions.
source: Upregulation of functional GABAA receptors as suggested by our data may decrease sensitivity to surprising events when outcome variability is high even under mostly stable conditions
evidence: Theoretical interpretation of gephyrin upregulation findings.

claim: Increases in GluN1 could support learning facilitation when the environment changes.
source: while increases in GluN1 could support learning facilitation when the environment changes.
evidence: Theoretical interpretation of GluN1 upregulation findings.

claim: Several psychiatric conditions such as anxiety, schizophrenia, obsessive compulsive and autism spectrum disorders, share pathological uncertainty processing as a core deficit.
source: Several psychiatric conditions such as anxiety, schizophrenia, obsessive compulsive and autism spectrum disorders, share pathological uncertainty processing as a core deficit, manifesting as a preference for stable, certain outcomes (Winstanley and Clark, 2016a, 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Recent studies have implicated mutations in the gephyrin gene as risk for autism and schizophrenia.
source: Interestingly, recent studies have similarly implicated mutations in the gephyrin gene as risk for autism and schizophrenia (Chen et al., 2014; Lionel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: Future research may address the role of gephyrin in surprise-driven learning and decision making under uncertainty in animal models of psychiatric disorders.
source: Future research may address the role of this synaptic organizer in surprise-driven learning and decision making under uncertainty in animal models of these disorders.
evidence: Suggestion for future research based on current findings and clinical relevance.

claim: Previous reports demonstrated that at least some subpopulations of OFC neurons carry expected uncertainty representations during option evaluation and outcome receipt.
source: Indeed, previous reports demonstrated that at least some subpopulations of OFC neurons carry expected uncertainty representations during option evaluation and outcome receipt (Li et al., 2016; van Duuren et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Subjects were 56 naïve male outbred Long Evans rats.
source: Subjects were 56 naïve male outbred Long Evans rats (Charles River Laboratories, Crl:LE, Strain code: 006).
evidence: Description of experimental subjects.

claim: All animals arrived at the facility at PND 70 (weight range 300–350 at arrival).
source: All animals arrived at our facility at PND 70 (weight range 300–350 at arrival).
evidence: Description of animal characteristics at study start.

claim: Vivaria were maintained under a reversed 12/12 hr light/dark cycle at 22°C.
source: Vivaria were maintained under a reversed 12/12 hr light/dark cycle at 22°C.
evidence: Description of housing conditions.

claim: Research protocols were approved by the Chancellor's Animal Research Committee at the University of California, Los Angeles.
source: Research protocols were approved by the Chancellor's Animal Research Committee at the University of California, Los Angeles.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.
